metadata.title: The Gate That Was Really Just a Vote
metadata.purpose: Show how a gate zeroes the composite when its condition fails while a vote merely subtracts a few points, so a decisive disqualifier quietly survives as a pretty-good score — and only a test that asserts exactly-zero tells a gate from a vote. Source: the-reallocation-engine/chapters/16-the-build-and-the-honest-run.md + Ch9 delegation
metadata.color_semantics: TEAL = gate behavior / the zero; CRIMSON = vote behavior / the surviving score; GOLD = the multiplier / key insight; SLATE = composite score bar

props.title: The Gate That Was Really Just a Vote

card.copy:
The Gate That Was
Really Just a Vote

beats.narration_text: The job posting expired six weeks ago. The role was filled. The system evaluated the posting anyway — skills match, location match, salary alignment, posting age. Skills and location score well. Salary scores well. Posting age scores poorly — call it a twenty-point deduction. Final composite: 72 out of 100. The system recommended pursuing the application. Here is the problem: a posting that is closed is not a weak posting. It is a zero. If your scoring system treated 'posting is dead' as a vote that subtracts twenty points, you do not have a filter. You have a suggestion box.

beats.narration_text: When a disqualifying condition reduces a composite score by a few points instead of zeroing it, what kind of control is that — and how do you tell the difference?

lines: When disqualifying conditions only subtract points,

card.copy:
When a disqualifier subtracts a few points
instead of zeroing the composite,
what kind of control is that?

beats.narration_text: A composite score is built from multiple signals. Each signal contributes to the total. The design question is: what role does each signal play? Some signals are votes — a higher value raises the composite, a lower value lowers it, but the composite can survive a bad vote and remain positive. Other signals are gates — if the gate condition fails, the composite becomes zero, regardless of how every other vote scored. The mistake is building something you call a gate, wiring it as a vote, and never testing whether it actually zeros the composite when it should. The gate becomes a leaky filter. Disqualified cases flow through.

beats.narration_text: The failure mode is invisible in normal operation. If most of your inputs satisfy all the gate conditions, the gate fires rarely. You review outputs that look reasonable. No case flags because no disqualified case has made it through yet, or the disqualified cases that did make it through looked plausible enough that no one caught them. The gate test requires deliberately sending in an input that should be disqualified and asserting that the composite is exactly zero — not just low, not under a threshold, not in the bottom decile. Zero. If the system returns 72, you have a vote. You do not have a gate.

beats.narration_text: The mechanism is the multiplier: a gate is wired as a multiplicative zero — fail the condition and the composite is zero; a vote is wired as an additive subtraction — fail the condition and the composite drops by a fixed amount. The wiring is the difference.
beats.image_description: A composite score bar — full width, filled in slate — with a 'liveness' input shown in two versions stacked vertically. Top version: liveness is wired as a multiplier (×0 when false), and the bar collapses completely to zero, the bar turning teal to show the gate behavior. Bottom version: liveness is wired as a subtraction (−20 when false), and the bar drops modestly, remaining filled in crimson at 72%, the disqualifying condition survived. A gold bracket between the two wiring diagrams is labeled 'THE WIRING IS THE DIFFERENCE'

beats.narration_text: The transform visualization. One composite score bar. Two wirings for the same liveness input. Wiring one: vote. The liveness condition fails — posting is closed. The scoring system subtracts 20 points. The bar drops from 92 to 72. The bar is crimson, still substantial, still in the top quartile for the day's batch. The system recommends the application. Wiring two: gate. The liveness condition fails — posting is closed. The gate fires as a multiplier: composite times zero equals zero. The bar collapses to empty, teal, exactly zero. The system discards the posting before it reaches the recommendation stage. Same input. Same 'liveness' label in the code. Two completely different outcomes depending on whether it was wired as a multiplication or a subtraction.

build.suggested: suggested prompt: The transform visualization. One composite score bar. Two wirings for the same liveness input. Wiring one: vote. The liveness condition fails — posting is close

beats.narration_text: The test that tells you which you have is a single assertion: send in an input where the gate condition is false, check the composite output, assert it equals exactly zero. Not less than ten. Not below a discard threshold you set at fifteen. Exactly zero. If the output is anything other than zero, the gate is a vote. This test is the minimum viable gate verification. It cannot be replaced by reviewing the output distribution, checking mean scores, or auditing a sample of recommended outputs. The only test for 'did the gate fire' is 'is the composite zero when the gate condition is false.'

beats.narration_text: The CAP250 test harness implication: every gate you document in your mode design must have a corresponding test that asserts the composite output equals exactly zero when the gate condition is false. This is not optional and it cannot be verified by reading the code. The code may look like a gate. The behavior may be a vote. The behavior is what the test checks. Document the gate condition, the input that triggers it, and the expected output: zero. If your test harness does not contain this test for every gate you designed, you have not verified you have a gate.

beats.narration_text: The Ch9 delegation lens: in an agentic pipeline, a gate is a delegation boundary. It is the point where the composite score is low enough that the system does not act — it escalates to a human, or it stops entirely. If the gate is wired as a vote, the delegation boundary is fuzzy. Cases that should stop at the gate and wait for a human decision flow through instead. The agentic system acts on cases it should not be acting on. The gate was the safety control. A vote is not a safety control.

beats.narration_text: The broader design principle: before you name a signal a gate, ask what the composite does when the gate fires. If the answer is 'it gets a low score,' the signal is a vote. If the answer is 'it becomes zero,' the signal is a gate. Name them correctly. Test them correctly. Do not call a vote a gate because the vocabulary sounds more decisive. The system does not know what you called it. It knows how you wired it.

beats.narration_text: A student's mode design has three stated gates: posting is live, visa requirement is compatible, application deadline has not passed. During CAP250 testing, the grader sends in a posting where the visa requirement fails — the role requires sponsorship and the student's profile says citizen-only preferred. The composite returns 61 out of 100. The gate did not fire. The grader sends in a posting where the deadline passed yesterday. The composite returns 54. Not zero. Not zero again. The student reads the test output and explains: 'The system still scored it lower for those conditions.' The grader writes: lower is not zero. A gate that returns 54 is a vote that subtracts 46. The student rewires both conditions as multipliers, re-runs the test harness. Both inputs now return zero. The CAP250 gate-behavior test passes. The submitted system has gates. The previous version had suggestions.

A vote merely lowers the composite, and a decisive disqualifier quietly survives as a pretty-good score. The only test that distinguishes them is an assertion that the composite equals exactly zero when the gate condition is false. Not low. Not below threshold. Zero.
